catalog_quote: [Patin 2016:290] To conclude this section, I will briefly discuss stress in Shingazidja, since stress will be of notable importance for some aspects of this study (see Section 3.3.1). As in several closely related languages such as Swahili (Ashton (1944), among many others), stress falls regularly on the penult of words. However, stress also relates to the Phonological Phrase in the sense that it seems to be strengthened on the penult of prosodic phrases: in (7a), for instance, the penult of tʃaí ‘tea’ is longer and more intense than the penultimate syllable of the preceding verb. To my knowledge, only one phonetic study has been conducted on stress in Shingazidja: Rey (1990). ... Thus, a detailed study of stress in Shingazidja still remains to be done. Such a study would have to determine the precise nature of the interactions between stress and tones. Indeed, numerous examples in my c…
sweep_summary: Four sweep items, all about the Shingazidja pitch-accent ('accent' = H-tone/metrical) system rather than plain word stress. New open fetch: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1989 (SLS 19, whole-volume PDF from IDEALS, text layer) — read in full; it analyses the nominal H-tone system with feet, Meeussen's Rule, final-syllable extrametricality and default H on the penult of toneless words; no separate stress statement; refines (does not contradict) the catalog's penult coding. Rey 1990 thesis: theses.fr record only (not accessible online), abstract read — the only experimental study (duration/F0/intensity) of Shingazidja accent, words 'oxyton ou paroxyton'; high acquisition priority. Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 (CLS 28) and Philippson 2005 (RMCA volume): no open copy anywhere checked (Crossref, Semantic Scholar, HAL, IDEALS, RMCA); library-print-only, medium priority. Also read from the sibling mwal1237 folder: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1997 ROA-176 (Swahili replaced tone with penultimate stress, Shingazidja retained tonal contrasts) and Philippson 1991 thesis (Comorian 'purement accentuelle', obligatory penult feet even without a marked syllable; Ngazidja feet grouped by two). Nothing read supersedes Patin 2016 as the deciding stress source; the caution that the 'accent' literature is about the pitch system stands.

new_statements.reading: First-hand elicited study, but of the pitch-accent (H-tone + metrical foot) system, not of stress: final syllables are extrametrical unless H-toned, and toneless words get their inserted prominence on the penult. It does not describe an independent word stress (the authors explicitly defer phonetic implementation, note 1 p.60). It is consistent with the catalog's penult coding as a default prominence, but the catalog's deciding source (Patin 2016 p.290: stress regularly on the penult, strengthened at the phrase penult, alongside the H-tone system) remains the only explicit stress statement read for this language.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at Patin 2016 p.290 in the held publisher PDF; locator correct. (2) The coding (fixed penult, weight-blind, coexisting with a privative H tone system) rests on the language's leading prosody specialist, and his later open papers fetched sources now (TAL 2018, SPiL Plus 2021) restate it: the penult (of the phrase) is the stressed syllable, lengthened, with tone/vowel-aperture interactions. Nothing found contradicts penult stress. sources.note: First-hand (elicited) analysis of the NOMINAL pitch-accent system: Proto-Bantu H tones retained, left-dominant unbounded quantity-sensitive feet built over H syllables in the phonological phrase, Meeussen's Rule, H realized on the last syllable of the foot; final syllable extrametrical unless H-toned; toneless words/phrases receive an inserted H (= metrical prominence) on the penult ('last visible syllable'). sources.citation: Cassimjee, Farida & Charles W. Kisseberth (1997/1998). Optimal Domains Theory and Bantu tonology: a case study from Isixhosa and Shingazidja. ROA-176 (published in Hyman & Kisseberth eds., Theoretical aspects of Bantu tone, CSLI).
sources.quote: In this section we examine the tonology of Shingazidja, a Bantu language, closely related to Kiswahili, which is spoken on the largest of the Comoros Islands, Ngazidja. Unlike Kiswahili, which lost the Proto-Bantu tonal system and replaced it with penultimate stress, Shingazidja has retained a system of tonal contrasts, and a complex surface tonal pattern
sources.note: Explicitly contrasts Swahili's penultimate stress with Shingazidja's retained tonal contrasts; H domains align with the right edge of the Prosodic Phrase, final syllable excluded (Nonfinality), so surface H lands on the phrase penult. Silent on whether Shingazidja also has a stress/lengthening on the penult; treats 'accent' as tone.

sources.quote: il apparait que la place de l'accent est predictible selon des regles phonologiques. L'analyse structuraliste genere la place de l'accent dans le mot, l'analyse metrique propose une hierarchie des accents dans la phrase. L'approche experimentale (en production et en perception) montre que l'accent n'est pas une propriete d'une syllabe, mais une relation entre syllabes: la relation tonique post-tonique semble privilegiee. Cette relation est fonction principalement de deux variables [...]: la structure syntaxique de l'enonce (phenomene de joncture), la place de l'accent dans le mot (mot oxyton ou paroxyton).
